The Austral pygmy owl (Glaucidium nana) is a small, cavity-nesting raptor of southern beech forests. Females of this species achieve an ultimate adult body mass of 76.15 grams [Wwi = 76.15 grams], a size dimorphism that is common among strigiforms and likely reflects the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. Newly hatched chicks emerge from the egg at a modest wet weight at birth of 7.0 grams [Wwb = 7.0 grams], a figure that underscores their altricial developmental state. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, recorded at 8.8 grams [Ww0 = 8.8 grams], is slightly heavier than the hatchling, reflecting the loss of albumen and shell material during embryonic development. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] have a developmental period culminating in hatching after approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days], though this incubation duration can vary by several days depending on local thermal conditions and parental attentiveness. This incubation period is consistent with values reported for other small forest owls in the Neotropics.

Under the thermal regime characteristic of active metabolic periods, measured here at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones governs the transition to independence. The time since birth at fledging, when the young bird leaves the nest cavity and achieves its first flight, occurs at 28.5 days [tx = 28.5 days], a relatively brief nestling period for a bird of its body size at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. During this period, the nestling undergoes a dramatic increase in mass, reaching a wet weight at fledge of 58.7 grams [Wwx = 58.7 grams], which is over eight times its birth mass. This rapid growth rate is fueled by intensive biparental provisioning of arthropod and small vertebrate prey. Following fledging, the time since birth at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation and the development of adult plumage, is estimated at 94.5 days [tp = 94.5 days], a value that falls within the broader range of 28 to 35 days reported for the onset of early reproductive behaviors in some captive studies, though the later figure accounts for full physiological readiness at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

The species exhibits a slow life-history pace relative to its small body size, a pattern characteristic of many tropical and temperate forest owls. The maximum recorded lifespan in the wild, assessed from long-term banding studies, is approximately 9.3 years [am = approximately 9.3 years], when measured under the typical body temperature conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This longevity is considerable for a bird of less than 100 grams and reflects low annual adult mortality rates in stable forest environments. Among males, the ultimate adult body mass is substantially lower than that of females, reaching a plateau of 66.15 grams [Wwi = 66.15 grams], a 15 percent reduction that is clearly linked to the reversed sexual size dimorphism seen in the genus Glaucidium. This dimorphism may reduce intraspecific competition for prey resources between the sexes, as the smaller males can exploit smaller insect prey that are less accessible to the larger females.

Under the thermoregulatory conditions typical of the species at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], seasonal reproduction in the Austral pygmy owl is tightly synchronized with the austral spring and summer abundance of insect and small mammal prey. Females lay a single clutch per year, with a reproductive output ranging from 1 to 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 5 eggs per clutch], and typically produce only one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually]. This modest brood size is typical of tropical and subtropical Strigidae and is thought to reflect the energetic constraints of rearing young in a temperate environment with a relatively short window of high prey availability. The time since birth at first brood, when a female produces her first successful set of offspring, occurs at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This indicates that first reproduction does not occur until the second calendar year of life, as juveniles fledged in one summer must survive the winter and attain full adult body condition before initiating breeding the following spring.

Comparative analysis within the genus Glaucidium reveals that the life-history parameters of the Austral pygmy owl occupy an intermediate position between those of smaller Old World pygmy owls and the larger Glaucidium species of Central and South America. The adult mass of 66.15 to 76.15 grams (66.15-76.15 grams) [Wwi = 66.15-76.15 grams] across the sexes places it squarely within the expected range for a medium-sized member of its genus. The initial egg mass of 8.8 grams [Ww0 = 8.8 grams] represents approximately 12 percent of the female's body mass, a substantial investment that is typical for cavity-nesting owls. The rapid attainment of a high fledging mass of 58.7 grams [Wwx = 58.7 grams] reflects the species' strategy of producing a relatively large, well-developed fledgling that can achieve early independence. This combination of slow adult somatic growth, delayed first reproduction, and high adult survival underscores the conservative life-history strategy that allows this small predator to persist across the fragmented landscapes of its Andean-Patagonian distribution.
